name: table-count
description: Number of Drizzle pgTable() definitions across shared/. The mature-machine north star is a SMALLER schema (<=450 tables); today's count is far above it. This strict down-only ratchet makes the schema monotonic: adding a table fails CI until the baseline is deliberately bumped (a conscious 'yes we need this'), and every consolidation lowers the baseline toward the target. Founder-chosen 'strict' 2026-07-16.
lastBumpNote: 760 -> 761 on 2026-08-12: outcomes -- the learning layer, closing the canonical loop (BI1, AA8, canonical law 9). decision_snapshots froze what was KNOWN and PREDICTED and scenarios froze the ARITHMETIC; nothing recorded what the world then DID, so an investor's own history was a pile of forecasts nobody ever graded. AA8 names the Decision->Outcome graph as a compounding moat precisely because a competitor can copy a screen but not a customer's calibration. VARIANCE IS NOT A COLUMN: it is computed as a pure projection over the scenario references the decision already froze, because a stored variance is a third number that can drift from the two it derives from, and improving it later would silently restate how good a past decision looked. decision_snapshot_id IS a real foreign key, unlike the deliberately unconstrained subject_id on evidence_claims / decision_snapshots / scenarios -- those must SURVIVE their subject, whereas an outcome without its decision is meaningless: there is nothing to compare it against and nothing it can teach. The FK is correct here for exactly the reason it was wrong there. NOT REUSING outcome_telemetry (shaped around AGENT performance -- agentActions, messagesSent, responseTime -- and carrying no decision reference) or outcome_calibrations (keyed by agent codename): both are the agent/founder learning loop, and BI76 is explicit that these are different things that must not collapse into one log. BI178 is honoured in the projection: an outcome is an OBSERVATION of what happened, not retroactive validation of the decision, so describeVariance never says a decision was good or wrong -- a record that scores decisions by their results teaches an investor to be lucky rather than right.
